reference: Fig. 2 presents the initial microstructure of the WAAM-fabricated C276 alloy. || To evaluate microstructural homogeneity across the build height, metallurgical cross-sections were extracted from the top, middle, and bottom regions and examined in the XY, YZ, and XZ planes, as illustrated in Fig. 2 . || The middle region exhibits well-aligned and relatively uniform dendrites ( Fig. 2 e), the bottom region shows a more cellular structure with limited secondary dendrite arms consistent with stronger heat extraction near the substrate ( Fig. 2 h), and the top region contains finer, shorter dendrites reflecting the altered thermal boundary conditions near the free surface and reduced reheating relative to mid-build ( Fig. 2 b). || EBSD orientation maps further show that WAAM samples contain much coarser grains than the wrought counterpart ( Figs. 1 a and 1 b), and that many grains exhibit a strong < 001 > alignment (arrows in Figs. 2 c, 2 f, and 2 i), consistent with preferred growth of the γ matrix along < 001 > under directional solidification. || Misorientation-to-mean maps ( Figs. 2 d, 2 g, and 2 j) reveal pronounced intragranular orientation gradients that manifest as low-angle (1°–10°) subgrain boundaries within large columnar grains (≥10° misorientation), indicating dislocation accumulation and subgrain boundary formation during cyclic thermal loading.

caption: LPBF single tracks of copper-coated diamond under varying laser power and scan speed. (a-c) Tracks produced at a scan speed of 250 mm/s with laser powers of 270 W, 320 W, and 370 W, respectively; (d-f) 375 mm/s; (g-i) 500 mm/s; (j-l) 625 mm/s; and (m-o) 750 mm/s.
reference: Here, the high in-plane thermal conductivity of diamond drains heat energy from the copper shell; thus, compared to monolithic metals, higher instantaneous power (or lower speed) is required to attain a comparable molten cross-section, but only up to the threshold beyond which recoil-driven fluctuations and Cu-diamond interfacial reactions begin to degrade bead quality. Fig. 4 shows that the stable conduction window sits around 150–220 J/mm 3 . || Below 120 J/ mm 3 the melt pool under-develops and beads fragment; above 250 J/mm 3 local over-melting and surface darkening/contrast changes appear. Fig. 4 a shows smooth, continuous track with uniform bead width, shallow penetration, and good wetting revealing conduction mode. || Fig. 4 b crosses into the over-energy regime where the crown becomes more convex with occasional surface roughness consistent with recoil-pressure ripples and transient vaporisation. Fig. 4 c accentuates this behaviour, with broader beads and more pronounced darkening/contrast change, indicating that absorption outpaces heat sinking into the diamond and substrate. || At 144 J/mm 3 ( Fig. 4 d) approaches the lower bound of continuity where the bead is continuous but thinner, signalling reduced pool lifetime. || Track in Fig. 4 e sits near the centre of the stability window and shows the best compromise of continuity, symmetry, and wetting.

reference: The evolution proceeds through six distinct regimes, corresponding to the micrographs revealed in Fig. 9 a-t . || At 74–111 J/mm 3 ( Fig. 9 a-b), the surface exhibits incomplete melting characterised by partially fused droplets, discontinuous Cu wetting, and irregular melt pools. || A dramatic shift occurs between 113 and 141 J/mm 3 ( Fig. 9 c-e), where porosity abruptly increases to 63–68% revealing the onset of a self-organised sub-micron lattice. || As energy increases to 143–184 J/mm 3 ( Fig. 9 f-i), the lattice begins to coarsen and thicken. || At 195–206 J/mm 3 ( Fig. 9 j-l), over-melting dominates, yielding a sharp porosity drop to 37%.
